claims.text: The baseline material is as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a density of 10.21 g cm−3.
The proposed intervention is alloying HfMoTaTiZr with a lightweight element such as aluminum.
Adding a lightweight element such as aluminum will decrease the density of HfMoTaTiZr.
The modified alloy will retain its room-temperature mechanical properties.
The modified alloy will retain its elevated-temperature mechanical properties at temperatures up to approximately 1000 °C.
Lightweight-element alloying may produce a stable solid solution.
Lightweight-element alloying may instead precipitate lightweight-element-based phases.
Introducing lighter elements reduces alloy density because they replace or supplement heavier constituents.
Lightweight-element addition may modify the alloy microstructure.
Lightweight-element addition may modify the alloy lattice parameters.
The predicted retained mechanical properties include strength.
The predicted retained mechanical properties include ductility.
The proposed applicability boundary extends from room temperature to 1000 °C under mechanical loading.
The experiment will compare density, tensile strength, and ductility for alloys containing varying concentrations of a lightweight element against as-cast HfMoTaTiZr at room temperature and 1000 °C.
The stated target is at least a 5% density reduction while mechanical properties remain within 10% of the as-cast values.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires both density reduction and retention of mechanical properties, but the rejection rule is phrased as a conjunction: it rejects only if density fails to decrease by 5% while properties are maintained. It does not clearly reject an alloy that achieves the density target but loses more than 10% of its mechanical properties.
